title: The present tense: four forms
topic: the present tense of regular verbs (pa'al): m. sg., f. sg., m. pl., f. pl.
why: Your first lesson on verbs: the Hebrew present tense has only four forms, depending on the gender and number of the subject, on the model of כּוֹתֵב (to write). It opens the unit "The present tense," reusing the pronouns and vocabulary from the unit "Introducing yourself."

{"lessons": ["

Four forms, depending on gender

In English, the present changes with the person: I write, but she writes. In Hebrew, the present doesn't care about the person but about the gender and number of the subject. The result: just four forms, like an adjective.

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
אֲנִי, אַתָּה, הוּא
ani, ata, hu		אֲנִי, אַתְּ, הִיא
ani, at, hi		אֲנַחְנוּ, אַתֶּם, הֵם
anakhnu, atem, hem		אֲנַחְנוּ, אַתֶּן, הֵן
anakhnu, aten, hen
כּוֹתֵב
kotev		כּוֹתֶבֶת
kotevet		כּוֹתְבִים
kotvim		כּוֹתְבוֹת
kotvot

אֲנִי (I) appears in two columns: a man says אֲנִי כּוֹתֵב, a woman says אֲנִי כּוֹתֶבֶת. The same goes for אֲנַחְנוּ (we).

הִיא כּוֹתֶבֶת.She writes. [hi kotevet]
אֲנַחְנוּ כּוֹתְבִים.We write. [anakhnu kotvim]

The pronoun is required: כּוֹתֵב on its own could mean \"I write,\" \"you write\" or \"he writes.\" So you always say who is writing: אַתָּה כּוֹתֵב, you write (to a man).

", "

The o-e pattern

Most simple verbs have a root of three consonants: כ־ת־ב for \"write.\" In the present, you slip the vowels o and e between them: ko-te-v. Then you add the endings you already know from nouns and adjectives: -et for the feminine, -im and -ot for the plural.

Three more verbs with the same pattern: לוֹמֵד (to learn, to study), עוֹבֵד (to work), אוֹכֵל (to eat).

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
לוֹמֵד
lomed		לוֹמֶדֶת
lomedet		לוֹמְדִים
lomdim		לוֹמְדוֹת
lomdot
עוֹבֵד
oved		עוֹבֶדֶת
ovedet		עוֹבְדִים
ovdim		עוֹבְדוֹת
ovdot
אוֹכֵל
okhel		אוֹכֶלֶת
okhelet		אוֹכְלִים
okhlim		אוֹכְלוֹת
okhlot

In the plural, the middle e disappears: כּוֹתְבִים is read kotvim, not \"kotevim.\"

נֹעָה לוֹמֶדֶת עִבְרִית בָּאוּלְפָּן.Noa is learning Hebrew at the ulpan. [No'a lomedet ivrit ba-ulpan]

English chooses between \"I eat,\" \"I'm eating\" and \"I usually eat.\" Hebrew has just one present form for all three.

", "

Reading and drinking: two small differences

קוֹרֵא (to read) ends in a silent א, which stays everywhere. שׁוֹתֶה (to drink) ends in a ה: in the feminine it becomes -a, and it disappears in the plural.

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
קוֹרֵא
kore		קוֹרֵאת
koret		קוֹרְאִים
kor'im		קוֹרְאוֹת
kor'ot
שׁוֹתֶה
shote		שׁוֹתָה
shota		שׁוֹתִים
shotim		שׁוֹתוֹת
shotot
אֲנַחְנוּ שׁוֹתִים קָפֶה.We're drinking coffee. [anakhnu shotim kafe]
נֹעָה וְדָנָה קוֹרְאוֹת עִתּוֹן.Noa and Dana are reading a newspaper. [No'a ve-Dana kor'ot iton]

A mixed group takes the masculine plural, even with just one man: נֹעָה וְאָבִי קוֹרְאִים, Noa and Avi are reading.

In the exercises, the verb to conjugate is given in parentheses in the infinitive, the dictionary form: לִכְתֹּב (to write). You'll study it in lesson 4; for now, just spot the three consonants of the root.
